title: I built a roleplay app alone in spared time
author: ApplicationDear9269
selftext:
Hey r/SideProject — I'm Sam. I just shipped Lyra ([https://lyra-ai.io](https://lyra-ai.io)), an AI roleplay/storytelling platform. But the part worth sharing here is the how, because I built it solo — and the whole game was using Claude Code to strip out the manual friction that normally drowns a one-person team.

I'm one person. No backend dev, no QA, no DevOps. Every manual step — every "remember to run this," every copy-paste deploy, every by-hand test — is friction that adds up until you stall. So I built my whole workflow around removing it:

🪄 Killing the manual busywork first

The trap of solo dev is death by a thousand small manual tasks: bumping configs, wiring boilerplate, regenerating clients, repetitive edits across files. I pushed all of it onto the AI so I'm spending my hours on decisions, not toil. The rule I settled on: if I've done it by hand twice, the third time the AI owns it.

design: use claude design then directly use it in claude code, this is big cause the native claude code is not able to produce production grade looking

🧵 Running multiple tasks in parallel

The bigger shift was treating it like a team I delegate to, not a chatbot. I'd have it building a feature in one isolated workspace while I reviewed something else in another — multiple independent threads at once, instead of me being the bottleneck on every line. A solo dev's scarcest resource is attention; this parallelizes it.

🚀 Deployment without a DevOps hire

Shipping used to be the scary part of going solo — one wrong command and you're down with no one to call. Now deploys are a single guard-railed action: push to staging, smoke-test for real, promote to production, with hard guards that refuse to run anything destructive against the live database. No manual checklist to forget a step on. I deploy several times a day without sweating it.

✅ Auto-testing instead of a QA team

This earned its keep. Instead of me clicking through the product by hand before every release, changes get exercised automatically against a real environment — and for the things that matter (the AI behaving, payments, safety) it runs live end-to-end tests and even drives a real browser like a user, then reports what broke. Catching regressions before users do, with zero manual QA.

🔍 A second set of eyes on every change

No teammate to review my PRs, so I have it do structured reviews — bugs, security holes, "you'll regret this in three months" stuff — before anything merges. It's caught real issues I'd have shipped.

What I ended up with

A live product where characters actually remember long conversations instead of forgetting the plot, mature stories aren't met with a lecture mid-scene, image gen is built in, and you get free credits to try it without a card. Built and run by one person who is not a 10x engineer — just someone who got ruthless about removing manual friction.

Honest take: the leverage is real but it's not magic. You still have to know what good looks like, review everything, and own the decisions. It made me faster, not optional.

Happy to go deep in the comments on the workflow — how I split tasks, the deploy guardrails, the testing setup. If you're a solo dev trying to ship something ambitious, that might be more useful than the product itself.

Product if you're curious: [https://lyra-ai.io](https://lyra-ai.io) (free credits on signup).
